extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemaking staff, regulatory affairs professionals, and public commenters (advocacy groups, regulated entities, individual commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing and processing public comments on federal rulemakings, with emphasis on identifying, authenticating, and managing AI-generated or mass comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and disclosure of AI-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection and disclosure of AI-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative framework requires identifying computer-generated comments and disclosing their presence; responds to growing capability of LLMs to produce variation in templated content and past large-scale fake comment campaigns. Implies agencies should have procedures and tools to detect AI-originated submissions and disclose findings in rulemaking materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authentication procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency authentication procedures
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are expected to adopt authentication procedures to verify commenter identity and legitimacy. This includes developing processes that help distinguish authentic individual submissions from fraudulent or automated ones and ensuring contact information is available to validate authorship when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking and reporting on mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking and reporting on mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should track occurrences of large-scale or coordinated comment campaigns and report on them. The Act emphasizes the need for transparency and record-keeping about mass campaigns (e.g., scope, provenance) to inform rulemaking and public disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for distinguishing substantive from non-substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for distinguishing substantive from non-substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act calls for clear standards to tell substantive, evidence-based comments apart from non-substantive or form/templated submissions. Agencies should focus on content quality (engagement with regulatory provisions, evidence) rather than sheer volume of similar text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource support for agencies dealing with mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Resource support for agencies dealing with mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation contemplates providing resources (funding, technical assistance) so agencies can manage high volumes of comments, implement authentication tools, and analyze comment substance at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clearly identified email and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain clearly identified email and contact information
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should provide clear contact details so their submissions can be authenticated and followed up on. This helps agencies verify that content is genuinely from the named individual or organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide content that is verifiably yours
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide content that is verifiably yours
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters are urged to submit material they can substantiate as their own work (not anonymous recycled or AI-mass-produced content). Verifiability supports the comment's credibility and helps agencies rely on its factual or experiential claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include personal context that authenticates identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Include personal context that authenticates identity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding personal details or context (relevant experiences, role, localized impacts) helps authenticate the author and increases the likelihood a comment will be treated as substantive and legitimate by agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with specific regulatory provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with specific regulatory provisions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments should address particular sections of a proposed rule, explain how the rule would affect the commenter or stakeholders, and provide targeted suggestions or evidence rather than general statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using AI to mass-produce substantively similar content
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using AI to mass-produce substantively similar content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act and commentary disfavor mass-identical or substantively similar AI-generated comments. Even if AI-assisted drafting is used, commenters should not produce large volumes of near-duplicate submissions that overwhelm agencies or dilute substantive input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop better authentication tools (agency action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop better authentication tools
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should invest in or adopt improved technical means to authenticate commenters (e.g., verifying contact details, metadata analysis, provenance tools) so they can more confidently determine whether submissions are from genuine individuals or orchestrated/automated campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create scalable approaches to evaluate comment substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Create scalable approaches to evaluate comment substance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given high comment volumes, agencies should build scalable evaluation methods (automated triage, prioritization heuristics, clustering) that surface substantive, evidence-backed comments while filtering or deprioritizing low-value mass submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish AI-assisted from AI-generated mass content
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish AI-assisted (legitimate) from AI-generated mass (problematic) content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework encourages nuanced treatment: AI-assisted comments that are human-authored and substantive remain legitimate, while mass-produced AI-generated comments intended to manipulate the process are problematic. Agencies should adopt criteria to make this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use semantic clustering rather than exact-match deduplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semantic clustering rather than exact-match deduplication
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are advised to employ semantic clustering techniques to group similar comments by meaning, instead of relying solely on exact-text matching, so that varied-but-duplicate AI-generated submissions can be identified while preserving legitimately unique perspectives that use different wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose how comments were processed in final rule preambles
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose how comments were processed in final rule preambles
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory transparency: agencies should explain in the rule preamble how they handled, filtered, and evaluated comments (including treatment of mass or AI-generated submissions), which supports accountability and public understanding of the decision-making record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content matters more
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive content matters more
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy trend emphasizes weighting content quality over quantity — detailed, evidence-based engagement with the rule is favored in evaluation of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity verification is becoming more important
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity verification is becoming more important
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical matter, agencies will increasingly rely on contact details and other authentication signals to assess the credibility and weight of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section-specific, evidence-based comments are favored
rubrics_metrics.description: Section-specific, evidence-based comments are favored
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that cite specific regulatory provisions and provide data, studies, examples, or concrete reasoning carry more weight than generic statements or slogans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass identical comments are dis-favored
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass identical comments are dis-favored
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form letters and coordinated identical submissions are less persuasive and may be deprioritized or treated as non-substantive, particularly when machine-generated; agencies are encouraged to separate or mark such campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted (but human-authored) comments remain legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-assisted (but human-authored) comments remain legitimate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of AI as a drafting aid is not inherently disallowed; what matters is that the resulting comment is human-authored, substantively original, and verifiable. Agencies should distinguish legitimate assistance from mass automated generation.
